input.content:
# Technical Plan

Approved on 18 October 2026, after a pressure test. The decision numbers (D-n) refer to `scope-and-decisions.md`, and the criterion IDs (S-n.n) refer to `user-stories.md`.

## Stack

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules), with no build step and no packages (D-15).

- **Prerequisite:** Node.js 22 or later (D-16). Node runs the tests and the local server.
- **Why:** the app is about 10 fields and some arithmetic. Every package or build step is one more thing that can fail on a reviewer's clean machine. With no dependencies, there's no `npm install` and no `node_modules`.
- **Browsers:** current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari. Every feature used, including BigInt and ES modules, is supported in all of them.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm start` | Serves `src/` at http://localhost:8080. The port can be changed with `PORT=3000 npm start`. |
| `npm test` | Runs every automated test with `node --test` |

`package.json` contains only `"type": "module"`, `"engines": {"node": ">=22"}` and the two scripts. It has no dependencies.

## Folder structure

```
firstname-lastname-calculator/
  README.md
  package.json
  scripts/
    serve.js              # static server for src/, Node's http module only (D-17, D-23)
  src/
    index.html            # markup; the form has autocomplete="off" (D-22)
    styles.css
    app.js                # UI only: state, events, copying engine output to the page (D-21, D-24)
    lib/                  # pure logic, no DOM, BigInt only (D-19)
      money.js            # text → BigInt cents; BigInt cents → "1,260.00"
      validate.js         # parsing and message precedence for every input type
      calc.js             # tip, even split, proportional allocation, receipt check
      messages.js         # every fixed message and template
      engine.js           # compute(state) → everything the screen shows
  tests/
    money.test.js
    validate.test.js
    calc.test.js
    engine.test.js        # acceptance criteria as tests, named by criterion ID
    messages.test.js      # every message matches user-stories.md exactly (D-25)
    manual-checklist.md   # every v1 criterion by ID, with Chrome and Firefox columns
  docs/
    app-roles.md
    jobs-to-be-done.md
    user-stories.md
    scope-and-decisions.md
    technical-plan.md
  transcripts/
  .github/workflows/pages.yml   # last priority (D-18)
```

## Architecture

`engine.js` exports `compute(state)`.

**`state` holds:**
- the selected mode
- the raw text of every field
- the tip choice, and the custom tip text
- the people list
- which fields the user has left

**`compute(state)` returns:**
- the error message for each field, or none
- which fields are outlined in red
- the results-area message, or the exact result lines for the current mode

**`app.js`** listens for input, leaving a field, clicks, add and remove, Reset and mode changes. On each one it updates `state`, calls `compute`, and copies the returned strings into the page. It never does arithmetic and never chooses wording.

**Rules for `app.js`:**
- Never recreate a field the user is typing in (D-21). Update only error text, outline classes and the results area.
- Rebuild people rows only when a row is added or removed, and put the cursor back where it was.
- Insert names and every other string as plain text, never as HTML (D-24).

## Money without floating-point errors

The rule is that money is a BigInt count of cents from input to display (D-6, D-19).

1. **Reading input.** The text is checked against a strict pattern. The whole part and the decimal part are joined as text and turned into BigInt, so `"1000.5"` becomes `100050n`. Then `"0.1"` plus `"0.2"` is exactly `30n`, shown as "0.30".
2. **Tip percentage.** It's held as BigInt hundredths of a percent, so 12.5% is `1250n`. The tip is `(subtotal × percent + 5000n) / 10000n`, which rounds exact halves up because every value is zero or positive.
3. **Even split.** `total / n` and `total % n`.
4. **Split by order.** Each share is `extra × ordered / sum` and its remainder is `extra × ordered % sum`, with the largest-remainder rule for leftover cents. S-6.10 proves this must be BigInt (D-20).
5. **Display.** The digits are grouped with commas by hand. `toLocaleString` is never used, so the result doesn't depend on the reviewer's language settings.
6. **Forbidden on money:** `parseFloat`, `Number()`, `toFixed()`, `Math.round()` and `toLocaleString()`. After each build step, `src/lib` is searched for these and any match is fixed.

## Testing

**Automated tests (`npm test`).** Every criterion with a calculated value or a message gets a test named with its ID, for example `S-6.10 leftover cent tie with large values`. Most criteria run through `compute(state)`, so the wording, the "Fix…" and "Fill in…" messages and the result lines are tested without a browser.

**Manual checklist (`tests/manual-checklist.md`).** Every v1 criterion is listed by ID, with a Chrome column and a Firefox column.
- Chrome gets a full pass of all 136 v1 criteria.
- Firefox gets a smoke pass of about 20 criteria, marked "smoke". That's at least one normal case and one error case per story, plus Reset, plus a reload check that no old values are restored.
- Each tick records the date and the browser version.

**Story status** follows the definition of done in `scope-and-decisions.md`.

| Story | Automated | By hand only |
|---|---|---|
| S-1 | Parsing, every message, precedence, results lines, "Fix…" and "Fill in…" logic | Error appears on leaving the field. Red outline before leaving (S-1.25). Reset |
| S-2 | Tip amounts, half-up cases, label formatting, tip precedence | Preset and "Custom" selection. The custom value is kept when switching back |
| S-3 | Every split, singular and plural wording, people parsing | Live update while typing. Reset |
| S-10 | Every value, across both modes | Fields shared between modes. Reset keeps the mode |
| S-5 | Amount validation, "Person N" labels and renumbering, names of only spaces | Add and remove rows. Disabled controls. 30-character cap, including paste |
| S-6 | Every value, including S-6.10 | Live updates |
| S-7 | Every warning and total-row message | Warning appears and disappears live |

Backlog stories (S-4, S-8, S-9) have no tests, because they are not built.

## Build order (D-27)

1. `src/lib` and its tests, including S-6.10 and the message check.
2. Diner: S-1, S-2, S-3.
3. Organiser: S-10, S-5, S-6, S-7.
4. The live URL, only if time remains.

If time runs out, the unfinished stories stay **Not implemented** and the README says so.

## For the README

**Assumptions:**
- The app must be served over HTTP, through `npm start`. Opening `index.html` directly shows a blank page.
- Node.js 22 or later is needed to start the app and run the tests.
- Only currencies with 2 decimal places are supported (for example PKR, USD, GBP, EUR). Currencies with none, such as JPY, are not.
- Commas and currency symbols are rejected, not stripped (D-9). Results show commas, so a result pasted back into a field gets an error message.
- Inputs are text fields with a decimal keyboard on phones, not number fields.
- On phones set to languages that use a decimal comma, the keyboard may not offer a decimal point.
- The 30-character name limit counts some emoji as 2 characters.
- Accessibility is best effort and not formally tested: fields are labelled, errors are linked to their fields, and results are announced when they change.

**Known risks and how they are handled:**
- **Floating-point money:** D-19, the search step, and test S-6.10.
- **Broken typing from live updates:** D-21, checked by hand.
- **Firefox restoring old values:** D-22, part of the Firefox smoke pass.
- **Untested browsers:** only the browsers actually tested are claimed. Safari and Edge are not claimed unless tested.
- **Time:** the build order and stop line in D-27.

Claude Code is recorded as D-28. There's also a `CLAUDE.md` for the project root, which Claude Code [loads automatically at the start of every session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md). It imports the user stories, the scope decisions and the technical plan, and sets the build rules: BigInt only, docs locked, one step at a time, and never marking a story Implemented itself. So every session starts with your full specification without you pasting it in.

## Set up the project

1. Create the folder `firstname-lastname-calculator`, put `docs/` and `CLAUDE.md` inside it, and run `git init`.
2. Open a terminal in that folder and run `claude`.
3. Run `/model` and note the model name for the README.
4. Run `/rename build-1`, which makes the session easy to find later.

## Your prompts

Type these yourself, in your own words if you like. The transcript must show your prompts exactly as typed, so what you write here is part of the evidence.

**Prompt 1: check it understands before it writes code.**
> Read CLAUDE.md and the documents it imports. Before writing any code, tell me in your own words: what you'll build in step 1 and which files; how you'll handle money; and anything in the documents that is unclear or contradictory, quoting criterion IDs. Don't write code yet.

**Prompt 2: build the logic and its tests.**
> Do step 1 only: package.json, src/lib, and tests for every v1 criterion that has a calculated value or a message, including S-6.10 and the message check. Run npm test and the forbidden-calls check, show me the output, then stop.

**Prompt 3: prove the BigInt test works.** This is your strongest evidence of checking the AI's work.
> Show me the S-6.10 test. Then temporarily switch the allocation to ordinary Numbers, run that test to show it fails, and put the BigInt version back. Run npm test again.

**Prompt 4: the Diner screens.**
> Do step 2: scripts/serve.js, index.html, styles.css and app.js for S-1, S-2 and S-3 only, plus tests/manual-checklist.md for all v1 criteria. Run npm test, tell me exactly how to start the app, and list which criteria I should check by hand first. Then stop.

After this, check those criteria in Chrome yourself.

**Prompt 5: the Organiser screens.**
> Do step 3: S-10, S-5, S-6 and S-7. Same end-of-step routine.

**Whenever a criterion fails, use this shape:**
> S-x.n fails. I did: … I expected: … I saw: … Write a failing test first if it can be tested, then fix it and tell me the cause.

These reports, with real IDs and real observations, are what reviewers mean by "mistakes you caught and fixed".

**Once every story's status is settled, the README:**
> Write README.md covering every item the brief lists, using the "For the README" section of technical-plan.md. Copy story statuses exactly from user-stories.md. Only name browsers I've confirmed. Leave placeholders for the model and time spent.

## Transcripts

- **Claude Code sessions.** Before ending or clearing a session, run `/export transcripts/session-02.md`, then `session-03.md` and so on. [`/export` saves the conversation as a plain-text file](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions.md). Claude Code's own session logs are deleted after 30 days by default, so export the same day.
- **This planning chat** becomes `session-01`. The Claude app has [no single-chat export, only a full account export](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9450526-export-your-claude-data). Go to Settings → Privacy → Export data in the web or desktop app. The download link arrives by email and expires after 24 hours, and you take this conversation from it unedited. It's worth starting that export now.

content.text:
> ## Documentation Index > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further. # Manage sessions > Name, resume, branch, and switch between Claude Code conversations. Covers `--continue`, `--resume`, `--from-pr`, the `/resume` picker, session naming, exporting transcripts, and where transcripts are stored. A [session](/docs/en/glossary#session) is a saved conversation tied to a project directory. Claude Code stores it locally as you work, so you can resume where you left off, branch to try a different approach, or switch between tasks. The [desktop app](/docs/en/desktop#work-in-parallel-with-sessions), [claude.ai/code](/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web), and the [VS Code extension](/docs/en/vs-code#resume-past-conversations) each keep their own session list, and the desktop app can also [resume a CLI session](/docs/en/desktop#coming-from-the-cli). This page covers the CLI. ## Resume a session Sessions are saved continuously to [local transcript files](#export-and-locate-session-data) as you work, so you can return to one after exiting or running `/clear`. Use these entry points: | Command | What it does | | :- | :- | | `claude --continue` | Reopens the most recent session in the current directory | | `claude --resume` | Opens the [session picker](#use-the-session-picker) | | `claude --resume ` | Resumes the named session directly | | `claude --resume ` | Resumes the session stored in the `.jsonl` [transcript file](#where-transcripts-are-stored) at that absolute path | | `claude --from-pr ` | Opens the session picker filtered to sessions linked to that pull request | | `/resume` | Switches to a different session from inside an active session |

Resume a running background session

When the conversation you resume with `claude --resume` or `/resume` belongs to a [background session](/docs/en/agent-view) that is still running, Claude Code opens the running session itself. With `--bg` on the command line, the resume is a [background dispatch](/docs/en/agent-view#from-your-shell) instead. Before v2.1.285, Claude Code refused and told you to open the session with `claude attach `, or to stop it with `claude stop ` first. * **From your shell**: `claude --resume ` runs [`claude attach`](/docs/en/agent-view#attach-to-a-session) on that session in the same terminal instead of loading the transcript itself. A prompt you pass on the command line, as in `claude --resume "check the tests too"`, goes to the session as its next turn first, and Claude Code prints `Sent your prompt to the background session (); opening it…` before attaching. `claude -p --resume "prompt"` typed at a terminal does the same, so `-p` doesn't keep that run non-interactive. Claude Code doesn't open the session when the command line has any of these: * Piped or redirected input or output * Flags that configure the session, such as `--permission-mode`, `--model`, or `--settings` * Flags that read the output, such as `--output-format json` or `--json-schema` * Flags that limit or rewind the run, such as `--max-turns` or `--max-budget-usd` With any of these, or when [agent view is turned off](/docs/en/agent-view#turn-off-agent-view), Claude Code sends nothing and exits with status 1, printing that the session is running in the background along with the `claude attach ` command that opens it, or telling you to find it in `claude agents` when it can't determine the ID. Add `--fork-session` to resume a copy of the conversation instead. To continue the conversation itself in a session of your own, with your flags applied, run `claude stop ` and then repeat the command. A prompt that starts with `/` or `!` isn't sent, and neither is any prompt while the session waits on your answer to a question. In both cases Claude Code doesn't open the session, and the message includes `Your prompt was not sent to it` with the reason. * **From inside a session**: `/resume` moves your current conversation to the background and attaches this terminal to the running session, printing `Opening "", running in the background (<id>)`. Press `←` on an empty prompt to return to agent view, which also lists the conversation you left. When the current conversation can't move to the background, for example because you're already attached to a background session or session persistence is off, `/resume` prints the `claude attach` command to run instead. ### What a resumed session restores When Claude Code loads a conversation from its transcript, the resumed session restores the conversation along with the state saved in it: * Conversation history: the full history, including tool calls and results. A tool that was still running when the previous process ended, for example in a crash, doesn't finish or run again when you resume. Claude sees the call marked as cut off before its result was recorded and is told to check whether it took effect before running it again, unless [`CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN`](/docs/en/env-vars#variables) is set. * Model: the session continues on the model it was using, except in the cases in [Setting your model](/docs/en/model-config#setting-your-model). * Agent: a session started with [`--agent`](/docs/en/sub-agents#invoke-subagents-explicitly) or the `agent` setting continues as that agent, keeping its tool restrictions and model. Pass `--agent` when resuming to pick a different one; for the system prompt in either case, see [System prompt flags in resumed conversations](/docs/en/cli-reference#system-prompt-flags-in-resumed-conversations). Claude Code looks for the agent in two places: the session's original directory, provided you have [trusted that workspace](/docs/en/permissions#project-allow-rules-and-workspace-trust), and then the directory you resume from, so a project-scoped agent still loads when you resume from another directory. If Claude Code doesn't find the agent in either place, the session resumes with the default tools and shows a [warning naming the agent](/docs/en/errors#session-agent-no-longer-available). * Permission mode: if you resume from a terminal with `claude --continue`, `claude --resume <session-id>`, or `claude --resume <name>` when the name matches one session, without `-p`, Claude Code restores the permission mode the session was in, except in the cases in [permission mode on resume](#permission-mode-on-resume), which also covers the session picker, `/resume`, and resuming with `claude -p`. Pass `--permission-mode` or `--dangerously-skip-permissions` to override the restored mode. * Active goal: a [goal](/docs/en/goal#resume-with-an-active-goal) that was still active when the session ended carries over; its turn count, timer, and token-spend baseline reset. * Scheduled tasks: [tasks that haven't expired](/docs/en/scheduled-tasks#limitations) are restored. Background Bash and monitor tasks aren't. * Background work: a [background subagent](/docs/en/sub-agents#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background), background Bash command, or [workflow](/docs/en/workflows) that ended with the previous process shows up in the resumed transcript as a note that it didn't finish. Claude Code doesn't start a turn from those notes; Claude reads them with your next prompt. Not every configuration flag from the original launch is restored. If the session depended on `--mcp-config`, `--settings`, `--plugin-dir`, `--fallback-model`, or directories added with `--add-dir`, pass them again when you resume; directories added mid-session with `/add-dir` aren't restored either, though the session picker still uses them to locate the session. The standard settings files, such as `settings.json` and `settings.local.json`, are re-read at launch, so configuration that lives in them doesn't need to be passed again. For `--system-prompt` and `--append-system-prompt`, see [System prompt flags in resumed conversations](/docs/en/cli-reference#system-prompt-flags-in-resumed-conversations). #### Permission mode on resume Which permission mode Claude Code starts a resumed session in depends on how you resume. The cases below apply when Claude Code loads the conversation from its transcript; when you [open a background session that is still running](#resume-a-running-background-session) instead, that session keeps the permission mode it is in. * Terminal: `claude --continue`, `claude --resume <session-id>`, or `claude --resume <name>` when the name matches one session, without `-p`. Claude Code restores the permission mode the session was in, except in the cases in the table. Pass `--permission-mode` or `--dangerously-skip-permissions` to override the restored mode. * Non-interactive: `claude -p --resume` or `claude -p --continue`. Claude Code starts the run in the permission mode a new `claude -p` run would start in, except that a session that ended in plan mode resumes in plan mode under the [conditions below](#resume-in-plan-mode-with-p). * VS Code: the extension's conversation panel. The table covers only a conversation that ended in plan mode; for the rest, see [resume past conversations](/docs/en/vs-code#resume-past-conversations). * Session picker at launch: a session you select from the [session picker](#use-the-session-picker), whether you opened it with `claude --resume` alone, `claude --from-pr`, or a name that matches more than one session. Claude Code starts the session in the permission mode it would start a new session in from the same command line, except that a session that ended in plan mode resumes in plan mode. If you pass `--permission-mode`, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, or `--fork-session`, Claude Code doesn't restore plan mode. No other stored permission mode is restored. * `/resume` inside a session, with or without an argument: the conversation you switch to continues in the permission mode your current session is in, except that a conversation that ended in plan mode resumes in plan mode, even if you launched Claude Code with `--permission-mode` or `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. If that conversation was already open earlier in this run of Claude Code, such as the conversation you started in or one you left with `/clear` or `/resume`, it continues in your current permission mode instead. If a [deny rule](/docs/en/permissions#manage-permissions) removes the [`ExitPlanMode`](/docs/en/tools-reference) tool, Claude can't present a plan for approval, so Claude Code doesn't restore plan mode. The session starts in the permission mode a new session would start in from the same command line. With `/resume`, the conversation continues in your current permission mode. Restoring plan mode on the non-interactive and VS Code paths requires Claude Code v2.1.246 or later. Each row names the permission mode the session ended in, which of the terminal, non-interactive, and VS Code paths you resume it by, and the permission mode Claude Code starts the resumed session in. | Session ended in | How you resume | Permission mode after you resume | | :- | :- | :- | | `bypassPermissions` | Terminal | The permission mode a new session would start in. To [bypass permissions](/docs/en/permission-modes#skip-all-checks-with-bypasspermissions-mode) again, enable it at launch with one of its launch flags or `permissions.defaultMode: "bypassPermissions"` in [user, `--settings`, or managed settings](/docs/en/settings-reference#permissions-defaultmode) | | `plan` | Terminal | Plan mode. With `--fork-session`, the permission mode a new session would start in | | `plan` | Terminal, when a deny rule removes `ExitPlanMode` | The permission mode a new session would start in | | `auto` | Terminal | `auto`, only when your account still meets the [auto mode requirements](/docs/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode) | | Manual | Terminal | Manual when a new session would start in auto mode from the [built-in default](/docs/en/permission-modes#which-mode-a-session-starts-in). When a `defaultMode` from a settings file [takes effect](/docs/en/permission-modes#which-mode-a-session-starts-in), Claude Code starts the resumed session in that mode instead | | `plan` | Non-interactive, under the [conditions below](#resume-in-plan-mode-with-p) | Plan mode | | Any mode | Non-interactive, in any other case | The permission mode a new `claude -p` run would start in | | `plan` | VS Code | Plan mode, with [the exceptions on the VS Code page](/docs/en/vs-code#resume-past-conversations) | <a id="resume-in-plan-mode-with-p" /> ##### Resume in plan mode with `-p` A `claude -p --resume` or `claude -p --continue` run resumes in plan mode only when all of these conditions hold: * You pass [`--permission-prompt-tool`](/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags) and don't pass [`--permission-prompts none`](/docs/en/headless#turn-off-permission-prompts-in-unattended-runs), so that Claude Code can present the plan for approval * You don't pass `--permission-mode` or `--dangerously-skip-permissions` * You don't pass `--fork-session` * The run isn't started through [channels](/docs/en/channels) * No [deny rule](/docs/en/permissions#manage-permissions) removes the `ExitPlanMode` tool ### Where the session picker looks Claude Code stores sessions per project directory. By default the session picker shows: * Sessions from the current worktree, including [background sessions](/docs/en/agent-view), which are marked `bg` in the list * Sessions started elsewhere that added the current directory with `/add-dir` Use `Ctrl+W` to widen to all worktrees of the repository or `Ctrl+A` to widen to every project on this machine. #### `/loop`, `-p`, Agent SDK, and background sessions Sessions whose first prompt was a [`/loop`](/docs/en/scheduled-tasks#run-a-prompt-repeatedly-with-%2Floop) command don't appear in the picker, and `claude --continue` skips them too. Running `/loop` later in a conversation doesn't hide the session. Claude Code leaves sessions created with [`claude -p`](/docs/en/headless) or the [Agent SDK](/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview) out of the session picker and out of `claude --continue`. You can still resume one by passing its session ID to `claude --resume <session-id>`. When you run [`claude -p --continue`](/docs/en/headless#continue-conversations), Claude Code includes `-p`, SDK, and `/loop` sessions. `claude --continue` opens a [background session](/docs/en/agent-view) that has finished, but not one that is still running; opening finished background sessions requires Claude Code v2.1.257 or later. If your most recent conversation is one you [moved to the background](/docs/en/agent-view#send-the-session-to-the-background) and it is still running there, Claude Code exits with `Your most recent conversation is running in the background` and that session's ID. Attach to the session from [`claude agents`](/docs/en/agent-view#attach-to-a-session), or run `claude --resume` to pick another one. #### Sessions in other worktrees and projects When you select a session from another worktree of the same repository, Claude Code resumes it in place; when the session's own worktree no longer exists, Claude Code [resumes it in your current directory](/docs/en/worktrees#resume-a-worktree-session). When you select a session from an unrelated project, Claude Code copies a `cd` and resume command to your clipboard instead. If that project's directory no longer exists, Claude Code resumes the session in your current directory rather than copying a `cd` command that would fail. Moving a session with [`/cd`](/docs/en/commands) relocates it to the new directory's project storage, so it appears in that directory's picker afterward. #### Resume by session ID or name You can run `claude --resume <session-id>` from any directory, so you can resume a session that started elsewhere or moved with [`/cd`](/docs/en/commands). Claude Code looks for the ID in this order: 1. The current project directory and its git worktrees 2. Every other project on this machine The cross-project search resolves the ID only when exactly one other project holds a transcript with messages for it, so a hand-copied duplicate makes Claude Code report not-found rather than resume an arbitrary copy. If no stored session matches the ID, Claude Code reports `No conversation found with session ID: <session-id>`. Resuming by name resolves across the current repository and its worktrees. Both forms look for an exact match and resume it directly even if it lives in a different worktree: | Command | Exact match | Ambiguous name | | :- | :- | :- | | `claude --resume <name>` | Resumes directly | Opens the session picker with the name pre-filled as a search term | | `/resume <name>` | Resumes directly | Reports an error; run `/resume` with no argument to open the session picker | ## Name your sessions Give sessions descriptive names so they're findable in the session picker and resumable by name. This matters most when you're working on several tasks in parallel. | When | How to set the name | | :- | :- | | At startup | `claude -n auth-refactor` | | During a session | `/rename auth-refactor`. The name also appears on the prompt bar | | From the session picker | Highlight a session and press `Ctrl+R` | | On plan accept | Accepting a plan in [plan mode](/docs/en/permission-modes#analyze-before-you-edit-with-plan-mode) gives the session a generated title based on the plan unless you've already named it | | From claude.ai or the Claude app | Rename a [Remote Control session](/docs/en/remote-control#connect-from-another-device); Claude Code applies the same name in the CLI. Requires Claude Code v2.1.221 or later | | From the desktop app | Rename a session in the [desktop app](/docs/en/desktop#work-in-parallel-with-sessions) | Once you name a session through a CLI route or from claude.ai, return to it with `claude --resume <name>` or `/resume <name>`; a desktop-app session resumes in the [desktop app](/docs/en/desktop#work-in-parallel-with-sessions). See [Resume a session](#resume-a-session) for how name resolution behaves across worktrees. Sessions you don't name still get two labels that Claude Code assigns. Only the generated title works as a resume handle: * Default display name: interactive sessions you never name still get a default display name when they start. Requires Claude Code v2.1.196 or later. The default combines the working directory's name with a two-character suffix, for example `my-app-3f`, and identifies the session in listings of running sessions, such as [agent view](/docs/en/agent-view) and `claude agents --json` output. The default isn't a resume handle. If you pass it to `claude --resume` or `/resume`, Claude Code doesn't find the session. * Generated title: if you don't name a session, Claude Code generates a session title for it. The title is a short summary of your first prompt, written by a background request to the small/fast model, normally a Haiku-class model. A `claude -p` run you start directly from a shell or script doesn't get one. Accepting a plan replaces the generated title with a title based on the plan. You can pass either title to `claude --resume` or `/resume`, and Claude Code resolves it the same way as a name you set. ## Use the session picker Run `/resume` inside a session, or `claude --resume` with no arguments, to open the interactive session picker. Use these keyboard shortcuts to navigate, search, and widen the list: | Shortcut | Action | | :- | :- | | `↑` / `↓` or `k` / `j` | Navigate between sessions | | `→` / `←` | Expand or collapse grouped sessions | | `Enter` | Resume the highlighted session | | `1` to `9` | Resume the session at that position in the list | | `Space` | Preview the session content. `Ctrl+V` also works on terminals that don't capture it as paste | | `Ctrl+R` | Rename the highlighted session | | `/` or any printable character other than `Space`, `j`, `k`, or a digit | Enter search mode and filter sessions. Paste a GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, or Bitbucket pull or merge request URL to find the session that created it | | `Ctrl+A` | Show sessions from all projects on this machine. Press again to return to the current repository | | `Ctrl+W` | Show sessions from all worktrees of the current repository. Press again to return to the current worktree. Only shown in multi-worktree repositories | | `Ctrl+B` | Filter to sessions from the current git branch. Press again to show all branches | | `Esc` | Exit the session picker or search mode | Each row shows the session name if you set one, otherwise the AI-generated session title, conversation summary, or first prompt, along with time since last activity, git branch, and file size. Sessions created with `/branch` or `--fork-session` get their own session IDs and appear as separate rows. When the picker finds more than one entry for the same session, it groups them under a single row. Press `→` to expand a group. If Claude Code can't load the session you select from the `claude --resume` picker, it prints [`Failed to resume the conversation`](/docs/en/errors#failed-to-resume-the-conversation) with a command to retry, then exits with code 1. From the `/resume` picker inside a session, Claude Code reports the failure and your current conversation keeps running. ## Branch a session Branching creates a copy of the conversation so far and switches you into it, leaving the original intact. Use it to try a different approach without losing the path you were on. From inside a session, run `/branch` with an optional name: ```text theme={null} /branch try-streaming-approach ``` If you omit the name, Claude Code names the new branch after the first prompt in the conversation. From the command line, combine `--continue` or `--resume` with `--fork-session`: ```bash theme={null} claude --continue --fork-session ``` The `/branch` confirmation prints two session IDs: the new branch you are now in and the original. The original is unchanged on disk and remains in the session picker; return to it with `/resume <original-name>` or by passing its ID to `/resume`. `/branch` copies the transcript and switches the running Claude Code process to write to it. That distinction determines what the branch inherits: | State | After `/branch` | | :- | :- | | Conversation history | Copied into the branch up to the point you ran `/branch` | | "Allow for this session" permission grants | Carried over; the branch runs in the same process, so your existing grants still apply. If you fork into a separate process with `--fork-session`, the new process starts without them and you re-approve there | | In-flight [background subagents](/docs/en/sub-agents#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background) and [background Bash commands](/docs/en/interactive-mode#background-bash-commands) | Keep running. Their output appears in the new branch you switched into, not in the original session | | [Remote Control](/docs/en/remote-control) connection | Stays connected. A phone or browser connected to the session follows you into the branch and keeps receiving new messages there | If you resume the same session in two terminals without forking, messages from both interleave into one transcript. For checkpoint-based rewind within a single session, see [Checkpointing](/docs/en/checkpointing). ## Manage context within a session These commands control what's in the context window without leaving the session: * **`/clear`**: start fresh with an empty context. Claude Code saves the previous session; resume it with `/resume`, or, in the same Claude Code process, from [the rewind menu's previous-session entry](/docs/en/checkpointing#rewind-past-a-cleared-conversation). With no argument, the new session keeps a name you set with `--name` or `/rename`, but not an AI-generated session title. To name the session you're leaving instead, pass the name, as in `/clear release-prep`; the new session then starts unnamed * **`/compact [instructions]`**: replace history with a summary, optionally focused on what you specify * **`/context`**: show what is currently consuming context For how compaction interacts with CLAUDE.md, skills, and rules, see the [context window guide](/docs/en/context-window). For strategies on when to clear versus compact, see [Best practices](/docs/en/best-practices#manage-your-session). ## Export and locate session data Run `/export` to open a menu that lets you copy the current conversation to your clipboard or save it as a plain-text file, with messages and tool outputs rendered as readable text. Pass a filename to skip the menu and write directly to that file. ### Access conversations from scripts `/export` produces a rendered transcript for a person to read. The interfaces below produce structured data for a script to parse: a JSON result from a run, the path to a session's transcript file, or a live stream of events. Pick by what triggers the script: * **Run Claude once and capture the result**: invoke `claude -p` with [`--output-format json` or `stream-json`](/docs/en/headless#get-structured-output) to capture the result, session ID, usage, and cost of a non-interactive run as structured JSON. * **Ask an existing session a question**: pass a session ID to [`claude -p --resume`](/docs/en/headless#continue-conversations) to send a follow-up prompt, such as a summary request, and capture the structured response. * **React to session events**: read the `transcript_path` field that [hooks](/docs/en/hooks#common-input-fields) and [status line commands](/docs/en/statusline#available-data) receive as input. A `SessionEnd` hook can archive the transcript when a session ends. * **Embed Claude in a TypeScript or Python app**: use the [Agent SDK](/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview) to receive each message programmatically. The example below uses the second interface. It sends a follow-up prompt to an existing session and reads the answer with `jq`: ```bash theme={null} claude -p --resume <session-id> --output-format json "summarize what we changed" | jq -r '.result' ``` ### Where transcripts are stored By default, Claude Code stores transcripts as JSONL at `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl`, where `<project>` is your working directory path with non-alphanumeric characters replaced by `-`. For a working directory whose converted name exceeds 200 characters, Claude Code truncates the name to 200 characters and appends a hash of the full path, so the directory name stays within filesystem limits. Each line is a JSON object for a message, tool use, or metadata entry. The entry format is internal to Claude Code and changes between versions, so scripts that parse these files directly can break on any release. To build on session data, use `/export` or the [script interfaces](#access-conversations-from-scripts) instead. The location, retention, and write behavior are configurable: | To | Set | Where | | - | - | - | | Move storage off `~/.claude` | [`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`](/docs/en/env-vars) | Environment variable | | [Name the `<project>` directory yourself](#name-the-project-directory-yourself) | [`CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME`](/docs/en/env-vars) | Environment variable | | Change the 30-day retention | [`cleanupPeriodDays`](/docs/en/settings-reference#cleanupperioddays) | `settings.json` | | Set an age limit for [Claude Desktop and Cowork transcripts](/docs/en/claude-directory#cleaned-up-automatically) | [`desktopSessionCleanupPeriodDays`](/docs/en/settings-reference#desktopsessioncleanupperioddays) | User settings, managed settings, or `--settings` | | Limit how large a `-p` or Agent SDK session's transcript file grows | [`CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC`](/docs/en/env-vars) | Environment variable | | Suppress transcript writes in all modes | [`CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY`](/docs/en/env-vars) | Environment variable | | Suppress writes for one non-interactive run | [`--no-session-persistence`](/docs/en/cli-reference) | CLI flag with `claude -p` | ### Delete session data Transcripts age out under the [retention sweep rules](/docs/en/claude-directory#cleaned-up-automatically). To delete a project's transcripts and related state sooner, run [`claude purge`](/docs/en/claude-directory#clear-local-data). If you delete a [background session](/docs/en/agent-view) with [`claude rm <id>`](/docs/en/agent-view#what-deleting-a-session-removes), its transcript stays on disk and remains available through `claude --resume`. ### Name the project directory yourself By default, Claude Code derives the `<project>` name from the whole working directory path. To choose the name yourself, set `CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME` alongside `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. Claude Code then stores that session's transcripts and [auto memory](/docs/en/memory#auto-memory) under your name. This suits a host that embeds Claude Code and gives each session its own config directory. Requires Claude Code v2.1.234 or later. For example, this launch keeps tenant A's data under `/srv/tenant-a` and names its project directory `work`: ```bash theme={null} CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=/srv/tenant-a CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME=work claude ``` Claude Code writes the session's transcripts to `/srv/tenant-a/projects/work/` and its auto memory to `/srv/tenant-a/projects/work/memory/`, whatever the working directory is. Three rules apply when you set it: * **Set `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` too**: the name doesn't vary with the working directory, so under the default `~/.claude` it would merge every project's transcripts and auto memory into one directory. Claude Code ignores `CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME` when `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is unset. * **Use 1-64 letters, digits, hyphens, or underscores**: don't use a Windows device name such as `con`. Claude Code ignores any other value and uses the derived name. * **Set it in the shell environment that starts `claude`**: Claude Code reads it once at startup from that environment, so an `env` block in a settings file can't set it. Once you've named a config directory's project directory, keep launching with that name. If you start Claude Code with the same `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` but without `CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME`, it reads and writes the derived directory again. The sessions stored under your name stay on disk: press `Ctrl+A` in the [session picker](#use-the-session-picker) to list sessions from every project directory under that config directory, the pinned one included, and whichever way you launch, [`claude --resume <session-id>`](#resume-a-session) finds a session stored under either name. ## See also These pages cover related session and parallelism mechanics: * [Worktrees](/docs/en/worktrees): run isolated parallel sessions on separate branches * [Checkpointing](/docs/en/checkpointing): rewind code and conversation to an earlier point * [Context window](/docs/en/context-window): what fills context and what survives compaction * [Non-interactive mode](/docs/en/headless): session behavior under `claude -p`

# How Claude remembers your project

> Give Claude persistent instructions with CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md files, and let Claude accumulate learnings automatically with auto memory.

Each Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window. Two mechanisms carry knowledge across sessions:

* **CLAUDE.md files**: instructions you write to give Claude persistent context. Claude can also read a repository's [`AGENTS.md` files](#agents-md) in place of CLAUDE.md
* **Auto memory**: notes Claude writes itself based on your corrections and preferences

This page covers how to:

* [Write and organize CLAUDE.md files](#claude-md-files)
* [Use an existing AGENTS.md](#agents-md) as your project instructions
* [Scope rules to specific file types](#organize-rules-with-claude/rules/) with `.claude/rules/`
* [Configure auto memory](#auto-memory) so Claude takes notes automatically
* [Troubleshoot](#troubleshoot-memory-issues) when instructions aren't being followed

## CLAUDE.md vs auto memory

Claude Code has two complementary memory systems. Both are loaded at the start of every conversation. Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a [PreToolUse hook](/docs/en/hooks-guide) instead. The more specific and concise your instructions, the more consistently Claude follows them.

| | CLAUDE.md files | Auto memory |

| **Who writes it** | You | Claude |
| **What it contains** | Instructions and rules | Learnings and patterns |
| **Scope** | Project, user, or org | Per repository, shared across worktrees |
| **Loaded into** | Every session | Every session (first 200 lines or 25KB) |

input.prompt: How does a user export their data or a conversation from Claude.ai? Can a single conversation be exported, or only all data? What format (JSON?), and how is it delivered (email link)? Any availability limits by plan or platform?

content.text:
**Exporting your data**

- Go to Settings > Privacy in the Claude web app or Claude Desktop, then click "Export data." The article doesn't offer an export option in the iOS or Android apps.
- The export covers account user information and chat history, which the article describes as "conversation data and the user data for your account."
- The article doesn't mention exporting a single conversation. It only describes a full export.

**Format and delivery**

- The article doesn't specify the file format, so it doesn't confirm JSON.
- After processing, you receive a download link by email at the address on your account. You must be signed in to download the data.
- The link expires 24 hours after delivery. To get a new one, repeat the export.

**Plan and platform limits**

- Individual Free, Pro, and Max users can export their data.
- On Team or Enterprise plans, members can export their own chats only after an owner turns on "Allow members to export their own data." Exports don't include the contents of uploaded files.
- Primary Owners export the whole organization's data from Organization settings > Data and privacy, not from their personal settings.

**Migration**

- You can't import exported data into another personal Claude account, and the article doesn't support moving data between personal accounts.
- If you're joining a Team or Enterprise organization, you can migrate your personal account directly into the organization instead of using an export.

# Tip and Bill Splitter: instructions for Claude Code

This is a take-home assignment. I am the candidate: I direct the work and check it, and you write the code. Reviewers will read the full transcript of our sessions, so be explicit about what you did, what you checked and what you were unsure of.

## Source of truth

@docs/user-stories.md
@docs/scope-and-decisions.md
@docs/technical-plan.md

`docs/app-roles.md` and `docs/jobs-to-be-done.md` give background. Read them if you need to know who the users are.

**The documents are locked.** Never edit anything in `docs/` unless I ask you to. If a criterion looks wrong, impossible, or in conflict with another, stop and tell me its ID. Don't work around it in code.

## Scope

- Build only the v1 stories: **S-1, S-2, S-3, S-10, S-5, S-6, S-7**.
- Never build S-4, S-8 or S-9, or anything listed under "Out of scope".
- Work in the build order in D-27. Do one step per request, then stop.

## Hard rules

- **No dependencies and no build step.** `package.json` has only `"type": "module"`, `"engines": {"node": ">=22"}`, and the scripts `start` and `test`.
- **Money is BigInt cents only (D-19).**
  - In `src/lib`, never use `parseFloat`, `Number()`, `toFixed()`, `Math.round()` or `toLocaleString()` on money.
  - Never mix BigInt and ordinary numbers.
  - Convert text to BigInt where input arrives, and BigInt to text for display.
- **Separation.**
  - `src/lib` never touches the DOM.
  - `src/app.js` contains no arithmetic and no message text. Every string it shows comes from `engine.js` or `messages.js`.
- **Exact wording.** Copy every message from `docs/user-stories.md` character for character, with straight apostrophes (D-25).
- **Live updates (D-21).** Never recreate a field the user is typing in. Rebuild people rows only on add or remove, and put the cursor back where it was.
- **Plain text only (D-24).** Insert names and all other strings with `textContent`, never `innerHTML`.
- **Form restore (D-22).** The form has `autocomplete="off"`.
- **Server (D-23).** `scripts/serve.js` serves only `src/`, sends `.js` as `text/javascript`, refuses paths outside `src/`, reads `PORT` (default 8080), and explains clearly when the port is busy.

## Tests

- `npm test` runs `node --test`.
- Every test name starts with the criterion ID it checks, for example `S-6.10 leftover cent tie with large values`.
- Keep `tests/manual-checklist.md` up to date. It lists every v1 criterion ID with a short description, a Chrome column and a Firefox column. About 20 criteria are marked "smoke" (D-27 and the definition of done).
- When I report a failing criterion:
  1. If it can be tested automatically, write a test that fails first.
  2. Fix the code.
  3. Run `npm test`.
  4. Tell me the cause.

## At the end of every step

1. Run `npm test` and show the pass and fail counts.
2. Run this check and show the output. Any match is a bug to fix:
   `grep -nE "parseFloat|Number\(|toFixed|Math\.round|toLocaleString" src/lib/*.js`
3. Summarise:
   - which files changed
   - what you tested
   - anything you couldn't do, or did differently from the plan, and why
   - any assumption you made
4. Never mark a story Implemented and never change a Status in `docs/`. I check the criteria by hand and tell you when to update a status.
5. Don't write the README until I ask.

It imports the user stories, the scope decisions and the technical plan, and sets the build rules: BigInt only, docs locked, one step at a time, and never marking a story Implemented itself. So every session starts with your full specification without you pasting it in.

## Set up the project

1. Create the folder `firstname-lastname-calculator`, put `docs/` and `CLAUDE.md` inside it, and run `git init`.
2. Open a terminal in that folder and run `claude`.
3. Run `/model` and note the model name for the README.
4. Run `/rename build-1`, which makes the session easy to find later.

## Your prompts

Type these yourself, in your own words if you like. The transcript must show your prompts exactly as typed, so what you write here is part of the evidence.

**Prompt 1: check it understands before it writes code.**
> Read CLAUDE.md and the documents it imports. Before writing any code, tell me in your own words: what you'll build in step 1 and which files; how you'll handle money; and anything in the documents that is unclear or contradictory, quoting criterion IDs. Don't write code yet.

**Prompt 2: build the logic and its tests.**
> Do step 1 only: package.json, src/lib, and tests for every v1 criterion that has a calculated value or a message, including S-6.10 and the message check. Run npm test and the forbidden-calls check, show me the output, then stop.

**Prompt 3: prove the BigInt test works.** This is your strongest evidence of checking the AI's work.
> Show me the S-6.10 test. Then temporarily switch the allocation to ordinary Numbers, run that test to show it fails, and put the BigInt version back. Run npm test again.

**Prompt 4: the Diner screens.**
> Do step 2: scripts/serve.js, index.html, styles.css and app.js for S-1, S-2 and S-3 only, plus tests/manual-checklist.md for all v1 criteria. Run npm test, tell me exactly how to start the app, and list which criteria I should check by hand first. Then stop.

After this, check those criteria in Chrome yourself.

**Prompt 5: the Organiser screens.**
> Do step 3: S-10, S-5, S-6 and S-7. Same end-of-step routine.

**Whenever a criterion fails, use this shape:**
> S-x.n fails. I did: … I expected: … I saw: … Write a failing test first if it can be tested, then fix it and tell me the cause.

These reports, with real IDs and real observations, are what reviewers mean by "mistakes you caught and fixed".

**Once every story's status is settled, the README:**
> Write README.md covering every item the brief lists, using the "For the README" section of technical-plan.md. Copy story statuses exactly from user-stories.md. Only name browsers I've confirmed. Leave placeholders for the model and time spent.

## Transcripts

- **Claude Code sessions.** Before ending or clearing a session, run `/export transcripts/session-02.md`, then `session-03.md` and so on. [`/export` saves the conversation as a plain-text file](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions.md). Claude Code's own session logs are deleted after 30 days by default, so export the same day.

**What was built**, all pure functions with no page code:
- **`src/lib/money.js`:** reads text straight into BigInt cents, and formats amounts and percentages for display.
- **`src/lib/validate.js`:** checks each kind of input, applying the documented order of error messages.
- **`src/lib/calc.js`:** the tip, the even split and the proportional split.

- **The forbidden-calls search.** It flagged one of my own comments that named a forbidden function. That was a false alarm, but it would recur at every step, so I reworded the comment and the search is now clean.

- **One of my test expectations.** For S-3.14 I first wrote "1 person pays 420.00". But 1,260.00 split 3 ways is exactly 420.00 each, so the line is "Each person pays 420.00". I fixed it before the first run.

**Differences from the plan:**
- **Test file names.** The criteria tests are in `diner.test.js` and `organiser.test.js` rather than one `engine.test.js`, so each file maps to a role. There's no separate `validate.test.js`, because every validation rule is already tested through the criteria. A small `tests/helpers.js` sets up test states.
- **Test names.** They use the full criterion ID, such as `S-3.2: 100.00 between 3 people is 33.34, 33.33, 33.33`. The example in your prompt was labelled "S-2", but splitting 100.00 three ways is criterion S-3.2.
- **Where it was built.** This step was done here in the Claude app (Claude Opus 5.5), not in Claude Code, which D-28 names as the build tool. Before you submit, the README and D-28 need to say which tool and model wrote which part, and this conversation's transcript then covers both the planning and this build step.

**Next step:** the Diner UI (S-1 to S-3), the local server, and the manual checklist.


The full output is in `test-output.txt`.

**What was built**, all pure functions with no page code:
- **`src/lib/money.js`:** reads text straight into BigInt cents, and formats amounts and percentages for display.
- **`src/lib/validate.js`:** checks each kind of input, applying the documented order of error messages.
- **`src/lib/calc.js`:** the tip, the even split and the proportional split.
- **`src/lib/messages.js`:** every message, copied exactly from the user stories.
- **`src/lib/engine.js`:** `compute(state)` turns the form's raw state into everything the screen will show. Reset, add person and remove person are included too, so their rules are testable without a browser.

**Coverage.** 133 of the 135 v1 criteria have an automated test. The two without one, S-5.20 and S-5.24 (the 30-character name limit when typing or pasting), depend on the browser's text field, so they go on the manual checklist.

**How I checked the tests:**
- **Three deliberate bugs, each caught.** I broke the code in three places and each time the tests failed. Reversing the tie-break failed 4 criteria, and rounding the tip down failed 3. Switching the split to plain Numbers failed **only S-6.10**, which proves that test does the job it was added for.
- **The forbidden-calls search.** It flagged one of my own comments that named a forbidden function. That was a false alarm, but it would recur at every step, so I reworded the comment and the search is now clean.

**Mistakes caught and fixed along the way:**
- **Criterion numbering.** My numbering script had labelled S-3's display rule as criterion S-3.1. I renumbered S-3 to run S-3.1 to S-3.16, corrected the v1 count to 135 in the technical plan, and logged it in the change log.
- **One of my test expectations.** For S-3.14 I first wrote "1 person pays 420.00". But 1,260.00 split 3 ways is exactly 420.00 each, so the line is "Each person pays 420.00". I fixed it before the first run.

**Differences from the plan:**
- **Test file names.** The criteria tests are in `diner.test.js` and `organiser.test.js` rather than one `engine.test.js`, so each file maps to a role. There's no separate `validate.test.js`, because every validation rule is already tested through the criteria. A small `tests/helpers.js` sets up test states.
- **Test names.** They use the full criterion ID, such as `S-3.2: 100.00 between 3 people is 33.34, 33.33, 33.33`. The example in your prompt was labelled "S-2", but splitting 100.00 three ways is criterion S-3.2.
- **Where it was built.** This step was done here in the Claude app (Claude Opus 5.5), not in Claude Code, which D-28 names as the build tool. Before you submit, the README and D-28 need to say which tool and model wrote which part, and this conversation's transcript then covers both the planning and this build step.

**Next step:** the Diner UI (S-1 to S-3), the local server, and the manual checklist.

  - **Phone width:** at 360px there's no sideways scrolling in either mode, and the table becomes one card per person.

I wrote failing tests first, and my first attempt at the fix was incomplete; the new test caught that before the browser run did.

content.text:
The UI is built on top of the engine, with both modes working: Split evenly and Split by order. Run `npm start`, then open http://localhost:8080.

**Your three requirements:**
- **Exact message wording.** The page shows only text that comes from `messages.js`, which a test checks word for word against the user stories. Fifteen messages were also read off the live page in the browser run, and all matched.
- **Never NaN, Infinity, undefined or a blank result.** A new test runs the engine on 20,000 random mixes of valid, invalid and extreme inputs and checks every string it produces, with no crashes. The browser run also scanned the page text in both modes.
- **Phone width and keyboard.**
  - **Phone width:** at 360px there's no sideways scrolling in either mode, and the table becomes one card per person.
  - **Keyboard:** the browser run used only Tab, arrow keys, Enter and typing. Adding a person moves focus to the new row, removing one keeps focus in the list, and focus is always visible.

**Verification:**
- **Unit tests:** 154 of 154 passing.
- **Browser checks:** 40 of 40 passing in headless Chromium, driven by keyboard.
- **Forbidden-calls search:** clean.
- **Server:** JavaScript is served with the right type, paths outside `src/` are refused, and a busy port gives the clear message.

**Bugs the checks caught:**
1. **An error message appeared too early.** I typed `1000`, left the field, came back and typed `a`, and the message showed before I left the field. That breaks the validation-timing rule. The engine tests missed it because they never modelled leaving a field that was valid. The fix was two engine functions, `editField` and `leaveField`, which only mark a field when it actually has a problem as you leave it. I wrote failing tests first, and my first attempt at the fix was incomplete; the new test caught that before the browser run did.
2. **The total row ran together on phones** as "Total3,000,000.00". I spotted it in the screenshot, then fixed the layout and confirmed by measurement that the total now lines up with the Owes column. The phone screenshot was taken **before** that fix, so it still shows the bug.

**Your manual checklist** is in `tests/manual-checklist.md`. It's generated from the user stories, so every criterion is worded exactly as in the document: all 135 v1 criteria, 19 of them marked smoke for Firefox. It adds six extra checks for keyboard use, phone width, reload, a pasted HTML name, never-NaN and uninterrupted typing.

**What's still yours to do:**
- **Hand checks.** Only Chromium was available here, so Firefox and the Firefox reload check need you. Under the definition of done, every story stays **Not implemented** until you've done the hand pass in Chrome and the Firefox smoke pass.
- **README note.** `PORT=3000 npm start` doesn't work as written in Windows Command Prompt or PowerShell, so the README needs to say that.

**Next step:** your Chrome pass with the checklist. Report any failure as "S-x.n fails: I did / expected / saw", and once stories pass, we update their statuses and write the README.

Empty: "Enter a tip percentage." | | 5 | 0, 1, 50, 51, 2.5 people | 1 person: "Each person pays 115.00". 50 people: "Each person pays 2.30". 0, 51 and 2.5 each gave "Number of people must be a whole number from 1 to 50." | | 6 | 0.01 between 2 people | The 10% tip on 0.01 rounds to 0.00, so the total is 0.01: "1 person pays 0.01", "1 person pays 0.00", "2 shares add up to 0.01". | | 7 | Cause an error, then fix it | While I was typing `100x`, the field went red and the results disappeared, with no message yet. **Severity, as I'd rank it:**
1. **#10, double-click Remove: high.** Silent data loss, easy to trigger, and it produces wrong amounts owed.
2. **#13, change-only updates: high, but rare.** The fields and results disagree, which is exactly the "wrong result" the brief warns about. Normal typing and Chrome's own autofill send typing events, so only some tools trigger it.

5. **#7, #8 and #9, misleading messages: low.** The app still rejects the input, so no wrong result.

content.text:
Five of the 15 attacks fail. **One produces a wrong result outright**, two more can lead to one, and **none crash**. As you asked, nothing has been fixed.

| # | Attack | What happened | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Floating point:** subtotal 0.1, tax 0.2, 0% tip, 1 person | "Total 0.30", "Each person pays 0.30". The amount is exact. | ✅ Pass |
| 2 | **Half-cent tips:** 0.01 at 50% (exactly half a cent), and at 49.99% | 50% gives a tip of 0.01 (rounded up); 49.99% gives 0.00. Both are correct. | ✅ Pass |
| 3 | **Largest possible bill:** 50 people each ordering 1,000,000, tax 1,000,000, tip 100% | Took 1ms with no overflow. Person 1 owes 1,040,000.00, and the Owes column adds up exactly to the 52,000,000.00 total. The warning correctly says the orders are 49,000,000.00 over the receipt. | ✅ Pass |
| 4 | **Leftover cents:** 0.49 tax spread over 50 equal orders of 0.01 | The first 49 people owe 0.02 and the last owes 0.01. That adds up to exactly 0.99. | ✅ Pass |
| 5 | **Huge or padded numbers:** `000…0001.00` (30 characters), and 5,000 nines | The first reads as 1.00. The second gives "Amount can't be more than 1,000,000.00." instantly, with no hang. | ✅ Pass |
| 6 | **Decimal comma:** `12,50`, then following the message's advice | The message says "Remove commas…". Doing exactly that leaves `1250`, which is accepted as **1,250.00, 100 times too much**, with no warning. | ❌ **Confusing message that leads to a wrong result** |
| 7 | **Space as a thousands separator:** `1 000`, or pasted with a no-break space | "Enter an amount using **digits**…". The user did type digits. | ❌ Confusing message |
| 8 | **Urdu digits from a phone keyboard:** `۱۰۰` or `١٠٠` (both mean 100) | Rejected with the same "digits" message. It's plausible on Urdu keyboards in Pakistan. | ❌ Confusing message |
| 9 | **Unicode minus:** `−5`, pasted from a document | "Enter an amount using digits…" instead of "Amount can't be negative." | ⚠️ Minor: a less helpful message, but still rejected |
| 10 | **Double-click "Remove"** on Person 1 of three rows | **Two rows are removed** (10 and 20), leaving only 30. The second click lands on the row that moved up into its place. | ❌ **Wrong result: data silently lost** |
| 11 | **"Add person" clicked 60 times** as fast as possible | It stops at exactly 50 rows: the button is disabled and "Up to 50 people." is shown. | ✅ Pass |
| 12 | **Edit after an error:** error on row 2, remove row 1, then add a row | The error stays with the right row (now Person 1), and the new row is clean. | ✅ Pass |
| 13 | **Autofill-style update:** a value set with only a "change" event, as some password managers and older autofill tools do | The field shows **500**, but the results still show **100.00** and "Each person pays 55.00". The page only listens for typing events. | ❌ **Wrong result: the screen contradicts itself** |
| 14 | **Reload, and Back then Forward**, with values entered | Both return to the opening state with nothing restored, so Chromium matches D-22. Firefox is still untested. | ✅ Pass |
| 15 | **30-character name with no spaces**, at 360px phone width | The page becomes **541px wide**, so it scrolls sideways at phone width. | ❌ Layout failure (it breaks the X-2 phone-width check) |

**Severity, as I'd rank it:**
1. **#10, double-click Remove: high.** Silent data loss, easy to trigger, and it produces wrong amounts owed.
2. **#13, change-only updates: high, but rare.** The fields and results disagree, which is exactly the "wrong result" the brief warns about. Normal typing and Chrome's own autofill send typing events, so only some tools trigger it.
3. **#6, decimal comma: medium.** The message itself steers the user into a 100× error.
4. **#15, long names at phone width: medium.** A layout bug only, but a reviewer is likely to try it.
5. **#7, #8 and #9, misleading messages: low.** The app still rejects the input, so no wrong result.

**What a fix would involve:**
- **#10, #13 and #15 are code bugs.** They break rules we already have: no wrong results, and the phone-width check (X-2). Fixing them doesn't change any documented behaviour.
- **#6 to #9 can't be fixed in code alone.** The messages and the accepted formats are fixed in the locked user stories (D-9 rejects commas on purpose). Changing them means amending the stories and the change log first. For example, #6 could get its own message for a comma followed by two digits, along the lines of "Use a point for decimals, e.g. 12.50".

Tell me which of these you want fixed and how. For #6 to #9, also decide whether to change the documented behaviour or record them as known limitations in the README.

input.content:
# Tip and Bill Splitter

A calculator that runs in the browser and works out a fair tip and who pays what when a group eats out together. It has two ways to split a bill:

- **Split evenly.** Enter the receipt and the number of people. The app shows the tip, the total and each person's share. When the total doesn't divide exactly, the extra cents are shown openly ("1 person pays 33.34, 2 people pay 33.33"), so the shares always add up to the bill.
- **Split by order.** For when one person paid for everyone. Enter what each person ordered. The app shares the tax, service charges and tip out in proportion to each order, shows what everyone owes, and warns if the orders don't add up to the receipt.

The receipt amounts and the tip are shared by both modes. Results update as you type, and invalid input gets a specific message instead of a result.

## Who it is for, and why I chose it

It's for groups of friends, family or colleagues settling a restaurant bill. Two kinds of user need different things:

- **A Diner** wants a fair tip and an even split, usually on a phone at the table.
- **A Bill Organiser** has already paid for everyone and needs to collect a different amount from each person, based on what they ordered. Any shortfall comes out of their own pocket.

When the bill arrives, three things go wrong in practice: people aren't sure what tip is fair; splitting evenly leaves leftover cents, so the shares don't add up; and working out who owes what from separate orders, plus a fair part of tax and tip, is slow and error-prone on a phone calculator.

I chose this calculator because the maths is simple but the edge cases (rounding, leftover cents, very small and very large amounts, invalid input) are exactly where real calculators get things wrong. That made it a good way to show careful requirements and testing in a small app.

## Product documents

1. [App roles](docs/app-roles.md): who uses the app
2. [Jobs to be done](docs/jobs-to-be-done.md): why they use it
3. [User stories with acceptance criteria](docs/user-stories.md): how the app helps, with every criterion numbered (for example S-6.10) and each story's status

Supporting documents:

- [Scope and decisions](docs/scope-and-decisions.md): what is in and out of scope, 36 numbered decisions (D-1 to D-36), the definition of done and a dated change log
- [Technical plan](docs/technical-plan.md): the stack, architecture and testing approach
- [Manual checklist](tests/manual-checklist.md): the hand checks in Chrome and Firefox, with results

## What is built

| Story | Role | Status |
|---|---|---|
| S-1 Enter the receipt amounts | Diner | Implemented |
| S-2 Choose a tip and see its amount | Diner | Implemented |
| S-3 Split the total evenly so the shares add up exactly | Diner | Implemented |
| S-10 Enter the receipt amounts when splitting by order | Bill Organiser | Implemented |
| S-5 List each person and what they ordered | Bill Organiser | Implemented |
| S-6 See what each person owes, with tax and tip shared in proportion | Bill Organiser | Implemented |
| S-7 Be warned when the amounts don't cover the bill | Bill Organiser | Implemented |
| S-4 Round everyone's share up to a whole amount | Diner | Not implemented (backlog) |
| S-8 Split a shared item between several people | Bill Organiser | Not implemented (backlog) |
| S-9 Copy a summary of who owes what | Bill Organiser | Not implemented (backlog) |

A story is marked Implemented only when it meets the [definition of done](docs/scope-and-decisions.md#definition-of-done-for-a-story):

- every acceptance criterion was checked by hand in Chrome
- its smoke criteria were also checked by hand in Firefox
- its automated tests pass

The backlog stories are fully specified but not built.

**Browsers checked by hand** (18 October 2026), with the results recorded in the [manual checklist](tests/manual-checklist.md):

- **Chrome 150.0.7871.256 (64-bit):** all 145 v1 criteria and 6 extra checks
- **Firefox 158.0:** the 21 smoke criteria and the 4 smoke extra checks

Edge and Safari were not tested, so they are not claimed. The app uses only standard features that all four browsers support (ES modules and BigInt).

There is **no live URL**. Publishing to GitHub Pages was planned as the last priority (D-18) and was not done.

## Prerequisites

- **Node.js 22 or later.** Developed and tested with Node.js 22.22.0. Node runs the local server and the tests. Check your version with `node --version`.
- **A current browser.** Checked in Chrome 150 and Firefox 158.

No paid accounts, API keys or cloud services are needed. There are no dependencies to install.

## Install and start

There is nothing to install: the project has no dependencies, so there is no `npm install` step and no build step.

```bash
cd firstname-lastname-calculator
npm start
```

Then open **http://localhost:8080** in your browser. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.

**If port 8080 is busy,** the server says so. Start it on another port instead:

| Terminal | Command |
|---|---|
| macOS or Linux | `PORT=3000 npm start` |
| Windows PowerShell | `$env:PORT=3000; npm start` |
| Windows Command Prompt | `set PORT=3000&& npm start` |

**Don't open `src/index.html` directly** from your file browser. Browsers block JavaScript modules on pages opened from disk, so the form would show but nothing would calculate. The app must be served over HTTP, which is what `npm start` does.

**Without Node.js,** you can run `python3 -m http.server 8080` inside the `src` folder. On some Windows machines Python serves `.js` files with the wrong type, which gives a blank page. `npm start` doesn't have that problem.

## Tests

```bash
npm test
```

This runs 161 automated tests with Node's built-in test runner. Every test name starts with the ID of the acceptance criterion it checks, for example `S-6.10: a tied leftover cent with large values goes to Person 1`.

| File | What it checks |
|---|---|
| `tests/diner.test.js` | The criteria of S-1, S-2 and S-3 |
| `tests/organiser.test.js` | The criteria of S-10, S-5, S-6 and S-7 |
| `tests/calc.test.js` | The arithmetic: tip rounding, even split, proportional shares |
| `tests/money.test.js` | Reading and formatting amounts, including 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.30 exactly |
| `tests/messages.test.js` | Every message in the app matches `docs/user-stories.md` word for word |
| `tests/safety.test.js` | 20,000 random inputs: no crash, and never NaN, Infinity, undefined or a blank result |

140 of the 145 v1 criteria have an automated test. The other five depend on the browser itself, so they are checked by hand only:

- S-1.34: a value filled in by autofill
- S-5.20 and S-5.24: the 30-character name limit, when typing and when pasting
- S-5.28: a double-click on Remove
- S-5.29: long names at phone width

The automated tests check the logic, not the page, so every v1 criterion was also checked by hand. The [manual checklist](tests/manual-checklist.md) is generated from the user stories by `node scripts/make-checklist.js`, which keeps the results already recorded when it is run again.

## How it works

- **Money is never a floating-point number.** Amounts are read as text straight into a whole number of cents, stored as JavaScript `BigInt`, and turned back into text only for display. So 0.10 + 0.20 is exactly 0.30.
- **Why BigInt and not ordinary whole numbers.** At large amounts, the split-by-order calculation multiplies values beyond the range ordinary JavaScript numbers hold exactly. Criterion S-6.10 is a real input where ordinary numbers give a leftover cent to the wrong person while the total still matches. Its test fails if BigInt is replaced.
- **Logic and page are separate.** `src/lib/` holds pure functions with no page code: `compute(state)` in `engine.js` returns every message and result line the page shows. `src/app.js` only copies that output onto the page, so the logic is fully testable without a browser.

```
README.md
package.json            scripts only: "start" and "test"; no dependencies
CLAUDE.md               instructions given to the AI coding tool
docs/                   the product documents listed above
scripts/
  serve.js              the local server for src/ (Node's built-in http module)
  make-checklist.js     generates tests/manual-checklist.md from the user stories
src/
  index.html, styles.css, app.js   the page
  lib/                  money.js, validate.js, calc.js, messages.js, engine.js
tests/                  the automated tests, helpers.js and the manual checklist
```

## AI tool and model

- **Tool:** Claude, in the Claude app, using its built-in code workspace (file editing, a shell, and a headless Chromium browser for checking the page).
- **Model:** Claude Opus 5.5.

All of the work happened in one conversation: the planning, the product documents, the code, the tests and the QA checks.

The plan was to build in Claude Code (decision D-28). In the end the code was written in the same Claude app conversation instead, and Claude Code was not used. The `CLAUDE.md` file holds the build instructions written for Claude Code during planning. Its rules were still followed throughout.

AI also drafted the product documents, which I directed, reviewed and corrected, as the transcript shows.

## Code changed by hand

None. All code was written by the AI tool. My part was to define the requirements, review the output, and check every acceptance criterion by hand in Chrome and Firefox. I reported failures and decisions back to the AI rather than editing code myself.

## Assumptions

- **Currency.** One currency with 2 decimal places, such as PKR, USD, GBP or EUR, and no currency symbol is shown. Currencies without decimals, such as JPY, are not supported.
- **Limits.**
  - Subtotal: 0.01 to 1,000,000.00
  - Tax and service charges: 0 to 1,000,000.00
  - Each person's order: 0.01 to 1,000,000.00
  - Custom tip: 0 to 100%, with at most 2 decimal places
  - People: 1 to 50, in either mode
  - Names: up to 30 characters
- **What is entered.** Tax and service charges are one optional amount, taken from the receipt. The tip is a percentage of the subtotal **before** tax and service charges, rounded to the nearest cent, with exact halves rounded up.
- **Leftover cents.**
  - **Split evenly:** the extra cents are shown openly as a higher share and a lower share, such as "1 person pays 33.34, 2 people pay 33.33". Shares are not tied to named people in this mode.
  - **Split by order:** each person's share of tax and tip is rounded down to the cent. The cents left over go one at a time to the people with the largest remainders, and ties go to the person higher in the list.

  In both modes, the amounts always add up exactly to the total.
- **Orders that don't match the receipt** are allowed. The app still shows what everyone owes, plus a warning that states the exact difference.
- **Input rules.**
  - Invalid input is rejected with a specific message, never silently corrected.
  - The only exceptions are spaces around a value, a trailing `%` on the tip, and Eastern Arabic and Urdu digits, which are read as 0 to 9.
  - Commas and currency symbols are rejected, not stripped, because a comma could be a thousands separator or a decimal point.
  - A comma used as a decimal point (`12,50`) gets its own message asking for a point.

## Known limitations

- **Commas in results.** Results show commas (`1,260.00`) for readability, but inputs reject commas. A result pasted back into a field gets a message asking to remove them.
- **Phone keyboards.** On phones set to a language that uses a decimal comma, the number keyboard may not offer a decimal point.
- **Name length.** The 30-character name limit counts some emoji as 2 characters.
- **Accessibility.** This is best effort and not formally tested. Fields are labelled, errors are linked to their fields, and the page was checked by hand with the keyboard only.
- **Fair tips.** The app suggests common tip levels (0%, 10%, 15%, 20%) but gives no advice on local tipping customs.
- **Telling people what they owe.** Copying a summary to send is a backlog story (S-9) and is not built.

## Session transcripts

The full transcript of the AI session is in `transcripts/`. It is exported unedited, apart from removing any passwords, keys or tokens.

```bash

npm start
```

# Publishes the app to GitHub Pages on every push to main (D-18).
# The tests run first, and the site is only published if they all pass.
# Only src/ is published: the page, its styles and its scripts.
# Local setup (npm start) stays the main way to run the app; this is a convenience copy.
#
# One-time setup in the repository: Settings → Pages → Build and deployment →
# Source: "GitHub Actions".

name: Deploy to GitHub Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Only one deployment at a time; a newer push waits for the current one to finish.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm test

  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: src
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
